Providence resident Catherine Bodner learned that the hard way, when a raccoon sunk its teeth into her right leg while she was pruning shrubs in her yard this summer. Bodner, 77, said she was in her backyard during daylight hours on Aug. 3 when she thought she heard a growl. She said to herself: “Is there a cat fight starting someplace?” “And the next thing I know, it’s attached to my leg,” Bodner recalled in an interview Thursday. “First, I was very frightened – and then I was mad as hell. That’s when I started to beat it. I smacked it in the head, and that made it drop off my leg.” She hit the raccoon in the head with her pruners several times and then ran inside, calling for her husband, she said. At The Miriam Hospital, she began a series of shots to treat rabies, as a precautionary measure, she said. Get Rhode Island News Alerts Sign up to get breaking news and interesting stories from Rhode Island in your inbox each weekday. Enter Email Sign Up The raccoon was never found, and therefore never tested for rabies, she said. “But when you’re attacked in broad daylight for no reason, you figure, ‘That’s rabid,’” said Bodner. The assumption is a fair one, especially this year: In 2026 so far, the number of animals that have tested positive for rabies, a potentially deadly disease, has nearly doubled in Rhode Island compared to years past, according to the state’s Department of Health. Health department data shows 46 animals tested positive this year so far – significantly more than the annual average of 25 between 2021 and 2025. On Wednesday, the department announced the latest cases: Two raccoons in Pawtucket, both found within a mile of a rabid raccoon recently found on Hope Street in Providence; and a raccoon in North Smithfield. Experts say there is no clear reason behind the trend. “We don’t know why it’s happening,” said Leanne Garzone, the animal control supervisor in North Smithfield, where the recent, rabid raccoon attacked a dog in a yard off of Black Plain Road on Sunday. “We don’t know why we’re seeing such an explosion.” What is known is that the Ocean State is not alone in experiencing the mysterious uptick. In September, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention issued a health advisory warning “multiple jurisdictions” across the United States had reported increases in human rabies exposures. Rabies is a viral disease that primarily affects the central nervous system and spreads through bites or scratches from an infected animal – typically raccoons, bats, skunks, and foxes, according to the CDC. The disease is preventable. People who have been exposed to rabies can receive a series of vaccines to prevent it from developing. Otherwise, rabies is fatal once signs of the illness – such as flu-like symptoms and discomfort around the bite mark – begin to show, health officials say. Each year, about 100,000 Americans are vaccinated against rabies after being potentially exposed to the disease, according to the CDC. Fewer than 10 deaths are reported in the United States annually. “But because it’s found in wildlife throughout the country (except for Hawaii), rabies poses a serious public health threat,” the CDC’s website states. This year, the CDC received 17 percent more rabies-related inquiries between July and August than it did during the same period in 2025, “including reports of mass exposure events,” or incidents involving more than one person. The agency also said there have been increases in the use of rabies vaccines compared to last year. “There’s a lot of unanswered questions,” said Dr. Suzanne Bornschein, Rhode Island’s state epidemiologist. Bornschein outlined a few of them during a recent phone interview: Is it that people are submitting more animals to be tested for rabies? Is there some sort of environmental factor in play, such as climate changes or habitat loss? Are there actually more animals with rabies, or are people more aware and more vigilant about reporting suspected cases than in the past? The key question, Bornschein said, is what does this increase represent? Rhode Island is hoping the CDC may be able to help. The state has requested what’s known as an “Epi-Aid” from the federal agency – an epidemic intelligence officer to analyze all of the numbers and cases, and try to make sense of what’s happening here, according to Bornschein. “We’re very interested because the problem with rabies is that if you don’t get treated after an animal exposure, it’s a fatal disease,” Bornschein said. A raccoon, caught in Forest Park in New York, Sept. 17, 2023.ANDRES KUDACKI/NYT In Massachusetts, officials said they aren’t quite seeing the alarming increases reported elsewhere. Dr. Catherine Brown, the Massachusetts state epidemiologist and public health veterinarian, said in a statement to the Globe there has been a “significant increase” in the number of bats submitted for rabies testing this year “with a small increase in the number positive.” “What this suggests is not that there is more rabies in bats this year, but we do think more people are finding information online that is helping them know to submit bats when it is appropriate to test them,” Brown said. The number of non-flying mammals that have been submitted and tested positive is ”similar to last year or lower than last year,” Brown said. A spokesperson for the Massachusetts Department of Health said rabies data for 2026 is not yet available. But data from 2025 shows Massachusetts had 999 bats submitted for rabies testing, of which 30 tested positive, while there were 1,690 terrestrial animals submitted for testing, and 80 of those tests came back positive. In North Smithfield, R.I., the raccoon in Sunday’s attack was the third rabid animal Garzone has encountered in 2026; the other two were a bat and another raccoon, she said. In contrast, the town had only one animal test positive in 2025 and two in 2024, state Department of Health data shows. “I was in a big city before,” said Garzone, who started working in North Smithfield within the past year, after previously working in Cranston. “If we had one case a year, that would be a big deal.” The rabies trend is not specific to one part of Rhode Island, she said. “We’re seeing them all over the state,” Garzone said. “So it’s not like they’re clustered in one area. We’re getting positives from Pawtucket. We’re getting positives from Providence. We’re getting positives from Warwick.” As of Wednesday, the state had recorded 25 rabid raccoons, 14 bats, four skunks, a cat, a coyote, and a woodchuck, officials said. Bornschein said Rhode Island is seeing more raccoons in particular with rabies this year, raising more questions: Are there actually more raccoons with rabies, or are there simply more raccoons coming in contact with humans? The “Epi-Aid” investigation is expected to provide insights into whether other states are seeing similar patterns, according to Bornschein. Garzone said it’s important pets are vaccinated for rabies. “Be aware,” she said. “Don’t feed the wildlife.” Nearly three months after a raccoon attacked her, Bodner still has bruises and swelling on her lower right leg. But, she said, “I’m not dead. I’m not foaming at the mouth.” What advice does she have for other Rhode Islanders concerned about rabid animals? “Carry a big stick,” she said. Bodner herself now has one emblazoned with the words: “For use in case of rabid raccoon attack.” “You have to be very aware of what’s around,” she said. Dass Entertainment N & M Andaman A&N Police Nicobar District Sports . Search for: Andaman Live Videos Home Andaman Media Delegation Visits Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor; Experts Share Insights on Rabies Prevention for Andaman and Vaccine Research Andaman Media Delegation Visits Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor; Experts Share Insights on Rabies Prevention for Andaman and Vaccine Research Sanjib Posted on 8 months ago Spread the love Sheekha Bureau Coonoor, March 13: A delegation of media representatives from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands visited the historic Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor on 12 March as part of a study tour aimed at understanding the institute’s work in vaccine research, manufacturing and disease prevention. The visit provided the delegation with an opportunity to learn about the institute’s scientific activities and its long-standing contribution to vaccine development in the country. During the visit, officials of the institute briefed the delegation about its research programmes, vaccine manufacturing processes and the role it has played in producing vaccines for major infectious diseases. The delegation also interacted with Dr. S. Sivakumar is the Director of the Pasteur Institute of India and senior scientists, who explained how vaccines were produced in the past and how the institute plans to expand its manufacturing capabilities in the coming years. One of the key topics discussed during the interaction was rabies, a viral disease that affects all warm-blooded animals and is mainly transmitted through the saliva of infected animals, most commonly through dog bites. Experts at the institute explained that once the rabies virus enters the body, it travels through the nervous system to the brain, where it multiplies and damages neural tissue. Once the central nervous system is affected, survival chances are extremely low, making prevention and timely treatment crucial. The experts also spoke about the situation in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, where rabies has not been reported so far. They advised that strict precautions must be maintained to keep the islands rabies-free. According to them, authorities should ensure that any animals brought from the mainland, particularly dogs and cats, are properly vaccinated and accompanied by valid vaccination certificates from recognized institutions. Proper verification of such certificates is essential before allowing animals to enter the islands. The scientists also highlighted the importance of immediate first aid in the event of an animal bite. Washing the wound thoroughly with plenty of water and seeking prompt medical attention for anti-rabies treatment can significantly reduce the risk of infection. The Pasteur Institute of India, located in Coonoor in Tamil Nadu, is one of the country’s premier government institutions dedicated to vaccine research and production. Functioning as an autonomous body under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, the institute has played a pioneering role in the development and supply of vaccines for several decades. The institute traces its origins to 1907, when it was established as the Pasteur Institute of Southern India following the death of a young woman who could not receive timely anti-rabies treatment. Over the years, it has achieved several milestones in vaccine research and manufacturing, including the production of anti-rabies vaccines, influenza vaccines and oral polio vaccines. In 2001, the institute developed a purified rabies vaccine derived from Vero cells for human use at an affordable cost, becoming the first government-controlled institution in India to do so. The move significantly helped reduce the cost of rabies vaccines in the country. Today, the institute operates modern facilities for the production of DPT group vaccines and has an installed capacity of around 130 million doses. Its laboratories are equipped with advanced technology and equipment used for large-scale vaccine production and research. The institute is also involved in academic activities, including doctoral research in microbiology, biochemistry and biotechnology. In addition, its anti-rabies treatment centre, established in 1907, continues to treat animal bite cases and collect important epidemiological data. Looking ahead, the institute plans to expand its capabilities further by establishing new biosafety level facilities for the production of viral, bacterial, conjugate and recombinant DNA vaccines. These developments are expected to strengthen India’s vaccine security and preparedness for future public health challenges. The visit provided the Andaman media delegation with valuable insights into vaccine research and public health preparedness, particularly in understanding the importance of maintaining strict preventive measures to keep regions like the Andaman and Nicobar Islands free from rabies. news.source_body_en: A media delegation from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands visited the Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor on 12 March 2026, as part of a study tour to learn about vaccine research and disease prevention. The visit focused on rabies, a viral disease transmitted through the saliva of infected animals, primarily via dog bites. Experts at the institute explained that rabies is fatal once it reaches the central nervous system, underscoring the importance of prevention and prompt treatment. They noted that rabies has not been reported in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and advised authorities to ensure that animals from the mainland are properly vaccinated and accompanied by valid certificates. The article was published on 29 October 2026 by ANDAMAN SHEEKHA.
news.content_zh: 2026年3月12日,来自安达曼和尼科巴群岛的媒体代表团访问了印度科诺尔的巴斯德研究所,作为一次学习之旅,了解疫苗研究及疾病预防的相关内容。此次访问重点介绍了通过感染动物唾液传播的狂犬病病毒性疾病,主要通过狗咬传播。研究所专家解释说,一旦狂犬病病毒进入中枢神经系统,就会致命,强调了预防和及时进行治疗的重要性。他们指出,狂犬病在安达曼和尼科巴群岛尚未有报告,并建议相关部门确保来自大陆的动物进行适当的疫苗接种,并携带有效的证书。成立于1907年的巴斯德研究所,在疫苗开发方面有着悠久的历史,继续治疗动物咬伤病例并收集流行病学数据。代表团深入了解了该研究所对公共卫生准备的作用及其扩大疫苗生产能力的计划。该文章由ANDAMAN SHEEKHA于2026年10月29日发布。

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 31, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Gene-Silencing Vector Shows Strong Protection Against Rabies in Mice by October 30, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 Gene-Silencing Vector Shows Strong Protection Against Rabies in Mice Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Rabies virus remains one of the most lethal human pathogens, and once its neurological symptoms appear, no effective treatment exists. A new study now reports that a gene-silencing approach delivered by a viral vector can sharply suppress rabies virus replication in laboratory cells and substantially improve survival in infected mice, both when administered before infection and when given after the virus has already entered the body. The research, published as a short communication in the journal Animal Diseases, focused on recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2, or rAAV2, as a delivery vehicle for short interfering RNAs, commonly called siRNAs. These small RNA molecules can silence specific genes by binding to their messenger RNA transcripts and triggering their degradation. The team designed siRNAs targeting two rabies virus genes: the G gene, which encodes the glycoprotein responsible for neuronal entry and transport, and the L gene, which encodes the RNA polymerase catalytic subunit essential for viral transcription and replication. The researchers first screened six candidate siRNAs, three against each target gene, in mouse neuroblastoma cells and baby hamster kidney cells infected with the rabies virus CVS-11 strain. Direct immunofluorescence assays showed that four of the candidates, si-G193, si-G672, si-G997, and si-L5055, significantly inhibited viral replication, with a marked reduction in fluorescent spots per field of view. Viral titer measurements confirmed that si-G997 and si-L5055 produced significantly lower titers than the negative control. Quantitative reverse transcription PCR revealed that all siRNAs targeting the G gene effectively reduced G messenger RNA levels in both cell types, while si-L5055 significantly decreased L messenger RNA levels. To verify that these effects reflected true gene knockdown rather than indirect antiviral activity, the team cotransfected human embryonic kidney cells with either si-G997 or si-L5055 together with plasmids expressing tagged rabies virus G or L proteins. Both siRNAs significantly reduced the expression of their respective target proteins compared with a scrambled negative control. Under infection conditions, the protein levels of the viral N and G proteins were reduced by both siRNAs, and the G protein was suppressed more markedly than the N protein. The authors attributed the poor performance of the other four siRNAs to differences in the thermodynamic properties of the target sequences and target site accessibility. Chemically synthesized siRNAs, although rapid in silencing target genes, are prone to degradation in the body and act only briefly. Viral vectors such as adenovirus, retrovirus, and lentivirus can deliver nucleic acids but often provoke strong host immune responses that generate neutralizing antibodies and weaken therapeutic effects. The researchers therefore turned to adeno-associated virus, which they describe as a relatively safe delivery system that supports long-term episomal expression in most tissues. Serotype 2 was chosen because most AAV vectors show predominant tropism for liver and muscle, whereas serotype 2 specifically targets the central nervous system, a property that fits the requirements of rabies virus research. The team encapsulated siRNA expression cassettes, each containing a CMV enhancer, a U6 promoter, and a shRNA coding sequence, into the rAAV2 vector, producing the constructs rAAV-G997 and rAAV-L5055. In HEK293T cells, these vectors significantly reduced the expression of the G protein and L protein, respectively. A CCK-8 assay showed that neither vector affected the viability of BHK-21 cells. When BHK-21 cells were transduced with the vectors 24 hours before rabies virus infection, both N and G protein levels decreased compared with a negative control vector, with the reduction in G expression more pronounced. In neuroblastoma cells transduced with rAAV-G997, G messenger RNA levels and viral titers remained consistently lower than in the control group at all time points examined, and rAAV-L5055 similarly reduced L messenger RNA levels and viral titers at every time point. The in vivo experiments used six-week-old Kunming mice divided into groups of ten. Three groups received intracerebral injections of rAAV2 at a dose of 2 × 1011 vector genomes per kilogram, followed 48 hours later by an intramuscular challenge with 1 × 105 focus-forming units of the CVS-11 strain. Among mice injected with rAAV-G997, rAAV-L5055, or a negative control vector before infection, the rAAV-G997 group maintained relatively stable body weight throughout a 21-day observation period, while survival rates reached 90 percent for rAAV-G997, 90 percent for rAAV-L5055, and 50 percent for the control. In a postexposure setting, mice received the same vectors 24 hours after viral challenge. The rAAV-G997 and rAAV-L5055 groups again showed relatively stable body weight changes compared with the control group, and survival rates were 88.9 percent for both treatment groups versus 55.6 percent for the control. A separate confirmatory experiment using 18 additional mice, six per group, measured viral loads in brain tissue on day 7 after infection. Both pretreatment groups exhibited significantly decreased viral loads in brain tissue compared with the negative control. The authors note that the lack of significant difference in efficacy between the two vectors suggests the strategy has a broad therapeutic window. The protective effect is attributed to two factors. Rabies virus primarily infects the central nervous system, and AAV2 exhibits natural tropism for neurons, enabling efficient transduction of the primary sites of viral replication when delivered directly to the brain. Intracerebral injection also bypasses the blood-brain barrier, delivering the therapeutic vector straight to the brain parenchyma. Consequently, even 24 hours after viral challenge, the vector-delivered siRNAs effectively suppressed viral replication within the central nervous system, an intervention that directly targets the intracellular viral life cycle and offers a prolonged therapeutic window that the authors say surpasses that of conventional biologics. The translational path faces considerable hurdles. The evaluations indicated that a relatively high viral dose is required for efficacy, which increases production costs. Owing to time constraints, the study was unable to assess the purity of the packaged rAAV2, and product-related impurities such as empty capsids may cause batch-to-batch variability and potentially exacerbate host immune responses. The authors conclude that rAAV2-mediated delivery of siRNAs targeting the rabies virus G and L genes can inhibit viral replication in vitro and provide significant protection in vivo, highlighting the potential of this platform as a therapeutic approach for rabies while acknowledging that addressing manufacturing and purity issues remains critical for any future clinical application. A new study now reports that a gene-silencing approach delivered by a viral vector can sharply suppress rabies virus replication in laboratory cells and substantially improve survival in infected mice, both when administered before infection and when given after the virus has already entered the body. The research, published as a short communication in the journal Animal Diseases, focused on recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2, or rAAV2, as a delivery vehicle for short interfering RNAs, commonly called siRNAs. These small RNA molecules can silence specific genes by binding to their messenger RNA transcripts and triggering their degradation. The team designed siRNAs targeting two rabies virus genes: the G gene, which encodes the glycoprotein responsible for neuronal entry and transport, and the L gene, which encodes the RNA polymerase catalytic subunit essential for viral transcription and replication. The researchers first screened six candidate siRNAs, three against each target gene, in mouse neuroblastoma cells and baby hamster kidney cells infected with the rabies virus CVS-11 strain. Direct immunofluorescence assays showed that four of the candidates, si-G193, si-G672, si-G997, and si-L5055, significantly inhibited viral replication, with a marked reduction in fluorescent spots per field of view. Viral titer measurements confirmed that si-G997 and si-L5055 produced significantly lower titers than the negative control. Quantitative reverse transcription PCR revealed that all siRNAs targeting the G gene effectively reduced G messenger RNA levels in both cell types, while si-L5055 significantly decreased L messenger RNA levels. To verify that these effects reflected true gene knockdown rather than indirect antiviral activity, the team cotransfected human embryonic kidney cells with either si-G997 or si-L5055 together with plasmids expressing tagged rabies virus G or L proteins. Both siRNAs significantly reduced the expression of their respective target proteins compared with a scrambled negative control. Under infection conditions, the protein levels of the viral N and G proteins were reduced by both siRNAs, and the G protein was suppressed more markedly than the N protein. The authors attributed the poor performance of the other four siRNAs to differences in the thermodynamic properties of the target sequences and target site accessibility. Chemically synthesized siRNAs, although rapid in silencing target genes, are prone to degradation in the body and act only briefly. Viral vectors such as adenovirus, retrovirus, and lentivirus can deliver nucleic acids but often provoke strong host immune responses that generate neutralizing antibodies and weaken therapeutic effects. The researchers therefore turned to adeno-associated virus, which they describe as a relatively safe delivery system that supports long-term episomal expression in most tissues. Serotype 2 was chosen because most AAV vectors show predominant tropism for liver and muscle, whereas serotype 2 specifically targets the central nervous system, a property that fits the requirements of rabies virus research. The team encapsulated siRNA expression cassettes, each containing a CMV enhancer, a U6 promoter, and a shRNA coding sequence, into the rAAV2 vector, producing the constructs rAAV-G997 and rAAV-L5055. In HEK293T cells, these vectors significantly reduced the expression of the G protein and L protein, respectively. A CCK-8 assay showed that neither vector affected the viability of BHK-21 cells. When BHK-21 cells were transduced with the vectors 24 hours before rabies virus infection, both N and G protein levels decreased compared with a negative control vector, with the reduction in G expression more pronounced. In neuroblastoma cells transduced with rAAV-G997, G messenger RNA levels and viral titers remained consistently lower than in the control group at all time points examined, and rAAV-L5055 similarly reduced L messenger RNA levels and viral titers at every time point. The in vivo experiments used six-week-old Kunming mice divided into groups of ten. Three groups received intracerebral injections of rAAV2 at a dose of 2 × 1011 vector genomes per kilogram, followed 48 hours later by an intramuscular challenge with 1 × 105 focus-forming units of the CVS-11 strain. Among mice injected with rAAV-G997, rAAV-L5055, or a negative control vector before infection, the rAAV-G997 group maintained relatively stable body weight throughout a 21-day observation period, while survival rates reached 90 percent for rAAV-G997, 90 percent for rAAV-L5055, and 50 percent for the control. In a postexposure setting, mice received the same vectors 24 hours after viral challenge. The rAAV-G997 and rAAV-L5055 groups again showed relatively stable body weight changes compared with the control group, and survival rates were 88.9 percent for both treatment groups versus 55.6 percent for the control. A separate confirmatory experiment using 18 additional mice, six per group, measured viral loads in brain tissue on day 7 after infection. Both pretreatment groups exhibited significantly decreased viral loads in brain tissue compared with the negative control. The authors note that the lack of significant difference in efficacy between the two vectors suggests the strategy has a broad therapeutic window. The protective effect is attributed to two factors. Rabies virus primarily infects the central nervous system, and AAV2 exhibits natural tropism for neurons, enabling efficient transduction of the primary sites of viral replication when delivered directly to the brain. Intracerebral injection also bypasses the blood-brain barrier, delivering the therapeutic vector straight to the brain parenchyma. Consequently, even 24 hours after viral challenge, the vector-delivered siRNAs effectively suppressed viral replication within the central nervous system, an intervention that directly targets the intracellular viral life cycle and offers a prolonged therapeutic window that the authors say surpasses that of conventional biologics. The translational path faces considerable hurdles. The evaluations indicated that a relatively high viral dose is required for efficacy, which increases production costs. Owing to time constraints, the study was unable to assess the purity of the packaged rAAV2, and product-related impurities such as empty capsids may cause batch-to-batch variability and potentially exacerbate host immune responses. The authors conclude that rAAV2-mediated delivery of siRNAs targeting the rabies virus G and L genes can inhibit viral replication in vitro and provide significant protection in vivo, highlighting the potential of this platform as a therapeutic approach for rabies while acknowledging that addressing manufacturing and purity issues remains critical for any future clinical application. analysis.brief_en: A new study published on October 30, 2026, reports that a gene-silencing vector, specifically recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 (rAAV2), can significantly suppress rabies virus replication in laboratory cells and infected mice. The research, conducted using Kunming mice, demonstrated that rAAV2 vectors targeting the G and L genes of the rabies virus reduced viral loads in brain tissue and improved survival rates. In pretreatment scenarios, survival rates reached 90% for both rAAV-G997 and rAAV-L5055, compared to 50% for the control group. In postexposure settings, survival rates were 88.9% for both treatment groups versus 55.6% for the control. The study highlights the potential of this platform as a therapeutic approach for rabies but acknowledges challenges in manufacturing and purity that must be addressed for clinical application.

In postexposure settings, survival rates were 88.9% for both treatment groups versus 55.6% for the control. news.content_zh: 一项于2026年10月30日发表的新研究报告称,一种基因沉默媒介,具体为重组腺相关病毒血清型2(rAAV2),能够显著抑制狂犬病病毒在实验室细胞和感染小鼠中的复制。该研究使用昆明小鼠进行,结果显示,针对狂犬病病毒的G和L基因的rAAV2 媒介可降低脑组织中的病毒载量并提高存活率。在预处理情况下,rAAV-G997和rAAV-L5055组的存活率分别达到90%,而对照组为50%。在暴露后处理情况下,治疗组的存活率分别为88.9%,而对照组为55.6%。该研究突显了该平台作为狂犬病治疗策略的潜力,但也承认在临床应用中需要解决制造和纯度方面的挑战。

analysis_zh.location_and_population: 该研究在实验室环境中进行,使用的是生物医学研究中的标准昆明小鼠品系。

analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 该研究显示,针对狂犬病病毒的G和L基因的rAAV2 媒介降低了脑组织中的病毒载量,并在预处理和暴露后情况下分别将存活率提高至90%和88.9%。对照组的存活率分别为50%和55.6%。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 该研究在体外和体内进行了实验,结果显示病毒复制被显著抑制。然而,作者指出,该技术的转化路径面临挑战,包括需要高病毒剂量以及可能影响批次一致性和免疫应答的包装rAAV2中的潜在杂质。

news.title: As rabies cases climb in Harford County, Humane Society vaccinates 360 pets
news.excerpt: As animal rabies cases in Harford County have soared in recent weeks, the local Humane Society vaccinated 360 pets during an event last weekend.

news.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Latino Voters World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Baltimore | News Weather Sports Video On WJZ Local Maryland WJZ at 9 Politics Consumer Business Health Entertainment First Alert Weather Radar & Maps Closings/Delays Weather Watchers All Sports CBS Sports HQ Ravens Orioles Terps College Sports Horse Racing Golf Odds WJZ at 9 Community MVP Volunteer with WJZ WJZ and the Baltimore Banner HealthyMD WJZ Investigates Black History Month About Us Meet The Team Contact Us Share A News Tip Nominate An MVP Advertise With Us Download The App Watch CBS News Local News As rabies cases climb in Harford County, Humane Society vaccinates 360 pets By Michelle Richardson October 28, 2026 / 12:52 PM EDT / CBS Baltimore Add CBS News on Google As animal rabies cases in Harford County have soared in recent weeks, the local Humane Society vaccinated 360 pets during an event last weekend. The Humane Society of Harford County's (HSHC's) low-cost vaccination clinic took place outside the Aberdeen Fire Department on Saturday. The clinic saw a total of 360 pets -- including 267 dogs, 91 cats, and two ferrets -- organizers announced in a news release. The event provided 300 rabies vaccines, as well as distemper and Bordetella. An additional 36 pets received microchips. The event comes after nearly 30 confirmed cases of rabies in animals were reported in Harford County this year. This rabies rate is the highest recorded in any community in Maryland, the release said. "When nearly 30 animals in our county have tested positive for rabies, the importance of keeping pets vaccinated really hits home," said Amanda Hickman, the executive director of HSHC. Jones Bel Air Subaru sponsored the clinic through the company's "Subaru Loves Pets" initiative, in which donations are made every October to the Humane Society through the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA). The funding helps cover costs for animal shelter adoptions and community pet vaccinations, according to the release. Employees from Jones Bel Air Subaru attended the clinic, greeting pet owners and giving away Subaru stuffed toys to the first 150 dogs in line. The Harford County Health Department was also at the clinic to provide information about their Oral Rabies Vaccination (ORV) program and educate the public about the disease. "With rabies cases at such concerning levels in Harford County, these clinics are more than a convenience – they're an important public health resource," said Hickman. "We're grateful to our partners for supporting this initiative to help safeguard public health and keep animals in loving homes," she added. news.content_zh: 在马里兰州哈福德县,哈福德县仁爱协会于上周末举办了一个低成本的疫苗接种诊所,以应对狂犬病病例的上升。该活动在阿伯丁消防局外举行,为360只宠物接种了疫苗,包括267只狗、91只猫和2只水貂,同时提供了300只狂犬病 疫苗疫苗,以及犬瘟热和博德特ella 疫苗疫苗。此外,还有36只宠物接受了微芯片植入。这一举措是在今年该县报告了近30例确认的动物狂犬病病例后进行的,这是马里兰州任何社区中最高的病例数。该诊所得到了琼斯贝尔艾尔丰田的支持,通过他们的“丰田关爱宠物”计划,并包含了关于狂犬病预防的公众教育。哈福德县卫生部门也参与其中,提供了关于其口服狂犬病 疫苗接种(ORV)计划的信息。此次活动突显了社区应对狂犬病 暴发的努力,并旨在保护宠物和公共卫生。

news.content_title: 狂犬病毒的分类学(三)_腾讯新闻
news.content: 前记 : 目前国际上关于狂犬病研究最权威、最全面的大型学术专著是 《 狂犬病的科学基础和管控( RABIES: SCIENTIFIC BASIS OF THE DISEASE AND ITS MANAGEMENT) 》,简称《 狂犬病 (RABIES) 》。该专著最新版( 第 5 版 )已于 2025年7月 面世。 本公众号已陆续将该专著第 4版(2020年版)的绝大部分内容翻译成中文。该专著最新版对旧版有较 多更新和 改进。本公众号将继续全文翻译该专著最新版的内容 , 将优先翻译新增加或更新较多章节的内容。 以下为该专著最新版 新增加的一章: 第 2 章 分类学 ( Taxonomy ) ( 三 ) 作者: Noël Tordo1, Peter J. Walker2 2.3 基因型与系统发生群的涌现 —— 以合乎逻辑的方式容纳日益增长的 狂犬病毒 属多样性 ( The emergence of genotypes and phylogroups to logically accommodate the growing diversity of Lyssaviruses ) 20 世纪 90 年代 PCR 技术的出现(见第 13 章),使研究得以从分析实验室适应株推进到在自然宿主中探索狂犬病毒属病毒。基因组序列数量迅速增加,促使病毒的区分与分类从血清学转向遗传学,并有系统发育分析作为支撑(见第 5 章)。 " 基因型 " ( genotype )一词被用来指称紧密的序列遗传簇,以区分 EBLV1 与 EBLV2—— 前者在遗传上与 DUVV 的亲缘关系比与 EBLV2 更近 (Bourhy et al., 1992) 。随后又提出了更量化的划分标准 (Bourhy et al., 1993; Kissi et al., 1995; Kuzmin et al., 2005) 。 1996 年从狐蝠科蝙蝠中分离出的 澳大利亚蝙蝠狂犬病毒( ABLV ) 也被确立为一个新的基因型,它是蝙蝠暴露后致死性人 类 病例的病因 (Fraser et al., 1996; Moore et al., 2010) 。 对中亚蝙蝠种群的主动监测进一步发现了新的狂犬病毒属病毒: 1991 年从 吉尔吉斯斯坦 的 狭耳鼠耳蝠 ( Myotis blythi ) 中分离出 阿拉万病毒( ARAV ) , 2001 年从 塔吉克斯坦 的 须鼠耳蝠 ( Myotis mystacinus ) 蝙蝠中分离出 苦盏病毒( KHUV ) (Kuzmin et al., 2003) 。 为了容纳并更好地分类狂犬病毒属中已鉴定病毒数量的不断增长, 2001 年依据遗传距离、系统发育关系、对单克隆抗体谱系的反应模式以及血清学交叉反应,将它们划分为两个系统发生群 (Badrane et al., 2001) 。系统发生群 I 包括 狂犬病 病毒( RABV )、欧洲蝙蝠狂犬病毒 1 型( EBLV1 )、欧洲蝙蝠狂犬病毒 2 型( EBLV2 )、杜文黑格病毒( DUVV )、澳大利亚蝙蝠狂犬病毒( ABLV )、阿拉万病毒( ARAV )和苦盏病毒( KHUV )。系统发生群 II 包括拉各斯蝙蝠病毒( LBV )和莫科拉病毒( MOKV )。 此后检出的狂犬病毒属病毒,依据其与这些系统发生群的系统发育关系进行归类 (图 2.2 ) 。系统发生群 I 新增了五个成员,其中多数最先在蝙蝠中检出,并有部分向其他哺乳动物物种传播: 2002 年在东西伯利亚贝加尔湖地区从 白腹管鼻蝠 ( Murina leucogaster ) 中分离出 伊尔库特病毒( IRKV ) (Kuzmin et al., 2005; Kuzmin and Tordo, 2012) ; 2010 年在德国从 纳氏鼠耳蝠 (Myotis nattereri ) 中分离出 博克洛蝙蝠狂犬病毒( BBLV ) (Freuling et al., 2011) ; 2014–2015 年在斯里兰卡从 狐蝠 ( Pteropus medius ) 脑中分离出 甘诺鲁瓦蝙蝠狂犬病毒( GBLV ) (Gunawardena et al., 2016) ; 2016–2017 年在 中国 台湾从濒死的 东亚家蝠( Pipistrellus abramus ) 中分离出 中国 台湾蝙蝠狂犬病毒( C TWBLV ) (Hu et al., 2018) 。 2017 年在芬兰从 布氏鼠耳蝠 ( Myotis brandtii ) 中分离出的 科塔拉赫蒂蝙蝠狂犬病毒( KBLV ),与 KHUV-BBLV-EBLV2 类群亲缘关系密切 (Nokireki et al., 2018) 。系统发生群 II 也因 希莫尼蝙蝠病毒( SHIBV ) 而得到补充 —— 该病毒于 2009 年从 肯尼亚 一处洞穴中死亡的 康氏菊头蝠 ( Hipposideros commersoni ) 分离得到,遗传上与 LBV 更接近 (Kuzmin et al., 2010) 。为归类另外三种狂犬病毒属病毒,有必要暂时增设第三个系统发生群(系统发生群 III ): 2002 年在俄罗斯西部从 普通长翼蝠 (Miniopterus schreibersii ) 中分离出的 西高加索蝙蝠病毒( WCBV ) (Hanlon et al., 2005; Kuzmin et al., 2005) ; 2009 年在坦桑尼亚从 非洲灵猫( Civettictis civetta ) 中分离出的 伊科马狂犬病毒( IKOV ) (Marston et al., 2012) ;以及 2011 年在西班牙加泰罗尼亚从一只死亡的 爪哇褶翅蝠 (Miniopterus schreibersii ) 中分离出的 莱里达蝙蝠狂犬病毒( LLEBV ) (Aréchiga Ceballos et al., 2013; Picard-Meyer et al., 2019) 。如今,潜在的新狂犬病毒属病毒仍在不断被鉴定:在南非蝙蝠中, 2015–2016 年在 纳塔尔小蝙蝠 ( Miniopterus natalensis ) 中发现 马特洛蝙蝠狂犬病毒( MBLV ) , 2021 年在 夜行施利芬 蝠 ( Nycticeinops schlieffeni ) 中发现 法拉蝙蝠狂犬病毒( PBLV ) 。 PBLV 属于系统发生群 I ,与 C TWBLV 亲缘关系最近;而 MBLV 属于系统发生群 III ,与 WCBV 的亲缘关系近于 LLEBV 和 IKOV (Viljoen et al., 2023) 。 中国 台湾的被动监测在一只 中华山蝠绒山蝠亚种 ( Nyctalus plancyi velutinus ) 中检出了 中国 台湾蝙蝠狂犬病毒 2 型 (Hu et al., 2022) ,斯洛文尼亚则在一只 栉鼠耳蝠 ( Myotis capaccinii ) 中检出了迪瓦查蝙蝠狂犬病毒,二者均属于系统发生群 I (Cerne et al., 2023) 。 图 2.2 基于归类于狂犬病毒属物种的 18 种病毒参考序列构建的系统发育树 。 推定的三个系统发生群的成员以 不同 颜色标示。作者非常感谢德国弗里德里希 · 勒夫勒研究所 Sten Calvelage 博士在构建该系统发育树方面给予的慷慨帮助。 本公众号相关文章的链接 三十年来全球发表狂犬病研究论文最多的国家和个人2021-6-10 权威的大型学术专著《狂犬病(Rabies)》最新版已面世 2020-06-30 一部跨越二十三年的"狂犬病百科全书" 2026-10-03 大型学术专著《狂犬病》2025年最新版的更新 2026-10-19 当代最著名狂犬病专家为学术专著《狂犬病》写的序言 2026-10-21 大型学术专著《Rabies》2025年第5版的《前言》2026-10-23 狂犬病毒的分类学(一) 2026-10-25 狂犬病毒的分类学(二) 2026-10-27

Walker2 2.3 基因型与系统发生群的涌现 —— 以合乎逻辑的方式容纳日益增长的 狂犬病毒 属多样性 ( The emergence of genotypes and phylogroups to logically accommodate the growing diversity of Lyssaviruses ) 20 世纪 90 年代 PCR 技术的出现(见第 13 章),使研究得以从分析实验室适应株推进到在自然宿主中探索狂犬病毒属病毒。基因组序列数量迅速增加,促使病毒的区分与分类从血清学转向遗传学,并有系统发育分析作为支撑(见第 5 章)。 " 基因型 " ( genotype )一词被用来指称紧密的序列遗传簇,以区分 EBLV1 与 EBLV2—— 前者在遗传上与 DUVV 的亲缘关系比与 EBLV2 更近 (Bourhy et al., 1992) 。随后又提出了更量化的划分标准 (Bourhy et al., 1993; Kissi et al., 1995; Kuzmin et al., 2005) 。 1996 年从狐蝠科蝙蝠中分离出的 澳大利亚蝙蝠狂犬病毒( ABLV ) 也被确立为一个新的基因型,它是蝙蝠暴露后致死性人 类 病例的病因 (Fraser et al., 1996; Moore et al., 2010) 。 对中亚蝙蝠种群的主动监测进一步发现了新的狂犬病毒属病毒: 1991 年从 吉尔吉斯斯坦 的 狭耳鼠耳蝠 ( Myotis blythi ) 中分离出 阿拉万病毒( ARAV ) , 2001 年从 塔吉克斯坦 的 须鼠耳蝠 ( Myotis mystacinus ) 蝙蝠中分离出 苦盏病毒( KHUV ) (Kuzmin et al., 2003) 。 为了容纳并更好地分类狂犬病毒属中已鉴定病毒数量的不断增长, 2001 年依据遗传距离、系统发育关系、对单克隆抗体谱系的反应模式以及血清学交叉反应,将它们划分为两个系统发生群 (Badrane et al., 2001) 。系统发生群 I 包括 狂犬病 病毒( RABV )、欧洲蝙蝠狂犬病毒 1 型( EBLV1 )、欧洲蝙蝠狂犬病毒 2 型( EBLV2 )、杜文黑格病毒( DUVV )、澳大利亚蝙蝠狂犬病毒( ABLV )、阿拉万病毒( ARAV )和苦盏病毒( KHUV )。系统发生群 II 包括拉各斯蝙蝠病毒( LBV )和莫科拉病毒( MOKV )。 此后检出的狂犬病毒属病毒,依据其与这些系统发生群的系统发育关系进行归类 (图 2.2 ) 。系统发生群 I 新增了五个成员,其中多数最先在蝙蝠中检出,并有部分向其他哺乳动物物种传播: 2002 年在东西伯利亚贝加尔湖地区从 白腹管鼻蝠 ( Murina leucogaster ) 中分离出 伊尔库特病毒( IRKV ) (Kuzmin et al., 2005; Kuzmin and Tordo, 2012) ; 2010 年在德国从 纳氏鼠耳蝠 (Myotis nattereri ) 中分离出 博克洛蝙蝠狂犬病毒( BBLV ) (Freuling et al., 2011) ; 2014–2015 年在斯里兰卡从 狐蝠 ( Pteropus medius ) 脑中分离出 甘诺鲁瓦蝙蝠狂犬病毒( GBLV ) (Gunawardena et al., 2016) ; 2016–2017 年在 中国 台湾从濒死的 东亚家蝠( Pipistrellus abramus ) 中分离出 中国 台湾蝙蝠狂犬病毒( C TWBLV ) (Hu et al., 2018) 。 2017 年在芬兰从 布氏鼠耳蝠 ( Myotis brandtii ) 中分离出的 科塔拉赫蒂蝙蝠狂犬病毒( KBLV ),与 KHUV-BBLV-EBLV2 类群亲缘关系密切 (Nokireki et al., 2018) 。系统发生群 II 也因 希莫尼蝙蝠病毒( SHIBV ) 而得到补充 —— 该病毒于 2009 年从 肯尼亚 一处洞穴中死亡的 康氏菊头蝠 ( Hipposideros commersoni ) 分离得到,遗传上与 LBV 更接近 (Kuzmin et al., 2010) 。为归类另外三种狂犬病毒属病毒,有必要暂时增设第三个系统发生群(系统发生群 III ): 2002 年在俄罗斯西部从 普通长翼蝠 (Miniopterus schreibersii ) 中分离出的 西高加索蝙蝠病毒( WCBV ) (Hanlon et al., 2005; Kuzmin et al., 2005) ; 2009 年在坦桑尼亚从 非洲灵猫( Civettictis civetta ) 中分离出的 伊科马狂犬病毒( IKOV ) (Marston et al., 2012) ;以及 2011 年在西班牙加泰罗尼亚从一只死亡的 爪哇褶翅蝠 (Miniopterus schreibersii ) 中分离出的 莱里达蝙蝠狂犬病毒( LLEBV ) (Aréchiga Ceballos et al., 2013; Picard-Meyer et al., 2019) 。如今,潜在的新狂犬病毒属病毒仍在不断被鉴定:在南非蝙蝠中, 2015–2016 年在 纳塔尔小蝙蝠 ( Miniopterus natalensis ) 中发现 马特洛蝙蝠狂犬病毒( MBLV ) , 2021 年在 夜行施利芬 蝠 ( Nycticeinops schlieffeni ) 中发现 法拉蝙蝠狂犬病毒( PBLV ) 。 PBLV 属于系统发生群 I ,与 C TWBLV 亲缘关系最近;而 MBLV 属于系统发生群 III ,与 WCBV 的亲缘关系近于 LLEBV 和 IKOV (Viljoen et al., 2023) 。 中国 台湾的被动监测在一只 中华山蝠绒山蝠亚种 ( Nyctalus plancyi velutinus ) 中检出了 中国 台湾蝙蝠狂犬病毒 2 型 (Hu et al., 2022) ,斯洛文尼亚则在一只 栉鼠耳蝠 ( Myotis capaccinii ) 中检出了迪瓦查蝙蝠狂犬病毒,二者均属于系统发生群 I (Cerne et al., 2023) 。 图 2.2 基于归类于狂犬病毒属物种的 18 种病毒参考序列构建的系统发育树 。 推定的三个系统发生群的成员以 不同 颜色标示。作者非常感谢德国弗里德里希 · 勒夫勒研究所 Sten Calvelage 博士在构建该系统发育树方面给予的慷慨帮助。 本公众号相关文章的链接 三十年来全球发表狂犬病研究论文最多的国家和个人2021-6-10 权威的大型学术专著《狂犬病(Rabies)》最新版已面世 2020-06-30 一部跨越二十三年的"狂犬病百科全书" 2026-10-03 大型学术专著《狂犬病》2025年最新版的更新 2026-10-19 当代最著名狂犬病专家为学术专著《狂犬病》写的序言 2026-10-21 大型学术专著《Rabies》2025年第5版的《前言》2026-10-23 狂犬病毒的分类学(一) 2026-10-25 狂犬病毒的分类学(二) 2026-10-27

analysis.time: The article discusses the 2025 release of the 5th edition of the authoritative book on rabies, with additional updates and findings from 2015–2016, 2021, and 2023. The publication date is 2026-10-30.
analysis.location_and_population: The article references various locations including Germany, Finland, China (Taiwan), South Africa, and Kenya, with populations involving bats and other mammals as hosts.
analysis.event: The article outlines the classification of rabies viruses into phylogroups based on genetic and phylogenetic data, including the identification of new members in system phylogroup I and III, and the addition of system phylogroup II with the discovery of SHIBV.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The article reports the identification of multiple new rabies virus variants, including ABLV, ARAV, KHUV, IRKV, BBLV, GBLV, CTWBLV, KBLV, SHIBV, WCBV, IKOV, LLEBV, MBLV, and PBLV. These viruses are primarily found in bats and other mammals, with some cases involving human exposure.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The classification of these viruses is based on genetic and phylogenetic analysis, with ongoing identification of new variants. The article is a review of the latest scientific findings and does not report any specific outbreak or response actions.

analysis.brief_en: This article discusses the classification of rabies viruses into phylogroups based on genetic and phylogenetic data. It highlights the 2025 release of the 5th edition of the authoritative book on rabies, which includes updates on the diversity of the Lyssavirus genus. The article reports the identification of several new rabies virus variants, such as Australian bat lyssavirus (ABLV), Aravan virus (ARAV), and Khosta virus (KHUV), primarily found in bats and other mammals. These viruses are categorized into three phylogroups, with system phylogroup I containing the majority of newly identified variants. The article also mentions the discovery of SHIBV in Kenya and the ongoing identification of new variants in South Africa and other regions. The findings are based on scientific research and do not indicate any specific outbreak or public health response. The content is a review of the latest scientific developments in rabies virus classification.

The article also mentions the discovery of SHIBV in Kenya and the ongoing identification of new variants in South Africa and other regions. The findings are based on scientific research and do not indicate any specific outbreak or public health response. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 31, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Rabies virus matrix protein stabilizes RGS4 to curb ferroptosis and aid replication by October 29, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Rabies virus matrix protein stabilizes RGS4 to curb ferroptosis and aid replication Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Rabies virus, the prototypical lyssavirus, suppresses neuronal ferroptosis through lipid droplet biogenesis, an immune evasion strategy previously identified by the research team. A new study now reports the mechanistic link between lipid droplet formation and ferroptosis regulation during infection, centering on a regulatory axis the authors describe as RGS4-HERC2-NCOA4-FTH. According to the study, rabies virus upregulates Regulator of G Protein Signaling 4 (RGS4), a ferroptosis-associated regulator, and this induction depends strictly on triglyceride synthesis and subsequent lipid droplet formation. Functionally, genetic or pharmacological inhibition of RGS4 elevates ferroptosis susceptibility, which in turn restricts viral replication. The mechanistic chain works as follows. When RGS4 is depleted, levels of HERC2 fall, impairing the assembly of branched K48/K63 ubiquitin chains on NCOA4. These chains are essential for NCOA4’s proteasomal degradation, so their loss stabilizes NCOA4. Stabilized NCOA4 then promotes ferritinophagy, the autophagic degradation of ferritin, leading to loss of ferritin heavy chain (FTH) and ultimately inducing ferroptosis. The lyssavirus matrix (M) protein directly counteracts this pathway. The researchers found that M protein inhibits RGS4 degradation via the Cys/N-degron system through incomplete autophagy, thereby stabilizing RGS4. Maintained RGS4 preserves HERC2 expression, promotes NCOA4 ubiquitination, and attenuates ferritinophagy. This reduces ferroptosis susceptibility and enables viral replication. The findings, reported in PLOS Pathogens, unveil what the authors describe as a novel lyssavirus-specific regulatory axis that modulates ferroptosis, highlighting the role of ferroptosis in lyssavirus infection and pathogenesis. The work is based on cell biological and mechanistic experiments described in the study, and the reported pathway links viral protein function to iron metabolism and autophagy during infection. Subject of Research: How the lyssavirus matrix protein stabilizes RGS4 to suppress ferroptosis during rabies virus infection Article Title: Lyssavirus matrix protein stabilizes RGS4 to suppress ferroptosis via incomplete autophagy and iron metabolic reprogramming Article References: Zhao, J., Chen, P., Sun, M., Liang, C., Fu, Z. F., Zhao, L., & Zhou, M. (2026). Lyssavirus matrix protein stabilizes RGS4 to suppress ferroptosis via incomplete autophagy and iron metabolic reprogramming. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 31, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Gene-Silencing Vector Shows Strong Protection Against Rabies in Mice by October 30, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 Gene-Silencing Vector Shows Strong Protection Against Rabies in Mice Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Rabies virus remains one of the most lethal human pathogens, and once its neurological symptoms appear, no effective treatment exists. A new study now reports that a gene-silencing approach delivered by a viral vector can sharply suppress rabies virus replication in laboratory cells and substantially improve survival in infected mice, both when administered before infection and when given after the virus has already entered the body. The research, published as a short communication in the journal Animal Diseases, focused on recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2, or rAAV2, as a delivery vehicle for short interfering RNAs, commonly called siRNAs. These small RNA molecules can silence specific genes by binding to their messenger RNA transcripts and triggering their degradation. The team designed siRNAs targeting two rabies virus genes: the G gene, which encodes the glycoprotein responsible for neuronal entry and transport, and the L gene, which encodes the RNA polymerase catalytic subunit essential for viral transcription and replication. The researchers first screened six candidate siRNAs, three against each target gene, in mouse neuroblastoma cells and baby hamster kidney cells infected with the rabies virus CVS-11 strain. Direct immunofluorescence assays showed that four of the candidates, si-G193, si-G672, si-G997, and si-L5055, significantly inhibited viral replication, with a marked reduction in fluorescent spots per field of view. Viral titer measurements confirmed that si-G997 and si-L5055 produced significantly lower titers than the negative control. Quantitative reverse transcription PCR revealed that all siRNAs targeting the G gene effectively reduced G messenger RNA levels in both cell types, while si-L5055 significantly decreased L messenger RNA levels. To verify that these effects reflected true gene knockdown rather than indirect antiviral activity, the team cotransfected human embryonic kidney cells with either si-G997 or si-L5055 together with plasmids expressing tagged rabies virus G or L proteins. Both siRNAs significantly reduced the expression of their respective target proteins compared with a scrambled negative control. Under infection conditions, the protein levels of the viral N and G proteins were reduced by both siRNAs, and the G protein was suppressed more markedly than the N protein. The authors attributed the poor performance of the other four siRNAs to differences in the thermodynamic properties of the target sequences and target site accessibility. Chemically synthesized siRNAs, although rapid in silencing target genes, are prone to degradation in the body and act only briefly. Viral vectors such as adenovirus, retrovirus, and lentivirus can deliver nucleic acids but often provoke strong host immune responses that generate neutralizing antibodies and weaken therapeutic effects. The researchers therefore turned to adeno-associated virus, which they describe as a relatively safe delivery system that supports long-term episomal expression in most tissues. Serotype 2 was chosen because most AAV vectors show predominant tropism for liver and muscle, whereas serotype 2 specifically targets the central nervous system, a property that fits the requirements of rabies virus research. The team encapsulated siRNA expression cassettes, each containing a CMV enhancer, a U6 promoter, and a shRNA coding sequence, into the rAAV2 vector, producing the constructs rAAV-G997 and rAAV-L5055. In HEK293T cells, these vectors significantly reduced the expression of the G protein and L protein, respectively. A CCK-8 assay showed that neither vector affected the viability of BHK-21 cells. When BHK-21 cells were transduced with the vectors 24 hours before rabies virus infection, both N and G protein levels decreased compared with a negative control vector, with the reduction in G expression more pronounced. In neuroblastoma cells transduced with rAAV-G997, G messenger RNA levels and viral titers remained consistently lower than in the control group at all time points examined, and rAAV-L5055 similarly reduced L messenger RNA levels and viral titers at every time point. The in vivo experiments used six-week-old Kunming mice divided into groups of ten. Three groups received intracerebral injections of rAAV2 at a dose of 2 × 1011 vector genomes per kilogram, followed 48 hours later by an intramuscular challenge with 1 × 105 focus-forming units of the CVS-11 strain. Among mice injected with rAAV-G997, rAAV-L5055, or a negative control vector before infection, the rAAV-G997 group maintained relatively stable body weight throughout a 21-day observation period, while survival rates reached 90 percent for rAAV-G997, 90 percent for rAAV-L5055, and 50 percent for the control. In a postexposure setting, mice received the same vectors 24 hours after viral challenge. The rAAV-G997 and rAAV-L5055 groups again showed relatively stable body weight changes compared with the control group, and survival rates were 88.9 percent for both treatment groups versus 55.6 percent for the control. A separate confirmatory experiment using 18 additional mice, six per group, measured viral loads in brain tissue on day 7 after infection. Both pretreatment groups exhibited significantly decreased viral loads in brain tissue compared with the negative control. The authors note that the lack of significant difference in efficacy between the two vectors suggests the strategy has a broad therapeutic window. The protective effect is attributed to two factors. Rabies virus primarily infects the central nervous system, and AAV2 exhibits natural tropism for neurons, enabling efficient transduction of the primary sites of viral replication when delivered directly to the brain. Intracerebral injection also bypasses the blood-brain barrier, delivering the therapeutic vector straight to the brain parenchyma. Consequently, even 24 hours after viral challenge, the vector-delivered siRNAs effectively suppressed viral replication within the central nervous system, an intervention that directly targets the intracellular viral life cycle and offers a prolonged therapeutic window that the authors say surpasses that of conventional biologics. The translational path faces considerable hurdles. The evaluations indicated that a relatively high viral dose is required for efficacy, which increases production costs. Owing to time constraints, the study was unable to assess the purity of the packaged rAAV2, and product-related impurities such as empty capsids may cause batch-to-batch variability and potentially exacerbate host immune responses. The authors conclude that rAAV2-mediated delivery of siRNAs targeting the rabies virus G and L genes can inhibit viral replication in vitro and provide significant protection in vivo, highlighting the potential of this platform as a therapeutic approach for rabies while acknowledging that addressing manufacturing and purity issues remains critical for any future clinical application. supplementary_news.content: Menu Log In Home E-Edition Subscribe News Front Page Neighbors Opinion On the Town expand child menu Calendar Sports Crime Community Business Podcasts Real Estate Obituaries Classifieds Photos Service Directory About Affiliate Content Advertising expand child menu Advertising Information Place Private Party and Rental Ads Here Legal Ads expand child menu Pricing Public Notices Place a legal ad Submission Forms expand child menu Letter to Editor Submit an Event Other Publications expand child menu Thousand Oaks Acorn Moorpark Acorn Camarillo Acorn Simi Valley Acorn Beyond The Acorn Contact Us Pick Us Up Privacy Policy Log In Account Home Other Publications Camarillo Acorn Moorpark Acorn Simi Valley Acorn Thousand Oaks Acorn Beyond The Acorn Submissions Letter to the Editor Submit an Event Subscribe Search for: Search Search for: Serving Agoura Hills, Calabasas, Oak Park & Westlake Village Saturday, October 31, 2026 News Front Page Neighbors Opinion Editorials Letters Columns Sports On the Town Calendar Crime Community Health Family Pets Schools Faith Obituaries Vacation Photos Business Real Estate Obituaries Agoura Hills and Surrounding Areas Obituaries Classifieds Online Ads About More Affiliate Content Advertising Advertising Information Place Private Party and Rental Ads Here Legal Ads Public Notices Place a legal ad Acorn Videos Contact Us Photos Pick Us Up Podcasts Awards Another rabid raccoon found in Westlake Village By The Acorn Staff on October 30, 2026 By Eamon Murphy eamon@theacorn.com FacebookTwitterPinterestEmailLinkedInCopy LinkPrintMessageShare A second rabid raccoon has been found in Westlake Village, this one appearing “sick and aggressive,” according to the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health. No residents or pets were exposed, and two people at a worksite who may have been exposed are receiving preventative care. The animal was found on Oct. 18 in a backyard on Dunraven Court in the city’s First Neighborhood, near where a previous rabid raccoon was reported on Sept. 17. That raccoon, described as “abnormally acting” but not aggressive, was the first in L.A. County to test positive for rabies since 1973. A state laboratory confirmed it had been infected with the bat strain of the virus. Testing to determine the variant involved in the second case is pending. 2026 has been a record-setting year for rabid bats in both L.A. and Ventura counties, with 77 and 32 detected so far, respectively. One such bat was found in First Neighborhood on Aug. 22, on a sidewalk outside the business center. The disease kills tens of thousands of people globally each year, though human rabies cases have been very rare in the United States since the eradication of the dog strain here through vaccination. The last locally acquired human case in L.A. County occurred in 1949, after a 24-year-old man was bitten by his rabid dog. Other variants of the rabies virus continue to circulate in wildlife and can infect and cause disease in any mammal. In a statement, L.A. County Health Officer Dr. Muntu Davis said the second rabid raccoon “is an important reminder to never touch, handle, or feed any wild animals, even when they appear healthy.” He urged residents to keep their distance from wildlife, report sick or unusually behaving animals to local animal control and ensure their pets are up to date on rabies vaccinations. For pickup and testing of sick or dead raccoons in the local area, residents can call the Agoura Animal Care Center at 818-991-0071. For more information, contact the L.A. County Veterinary Public Health Program at 213-288-7060. supplementary_news.content: Open menu NTD Television U.S.ChinaWorldPoliticsHealthBusinessEntertainmentSports More ●LIVE search EN▼ NTD Television Health News US Rabies Surge Prompts Public Health Warning As recently as Oct. 11, the Pasadena Public Health Department in California reported finding an infected bat along East Green Street between South Marengo and South Euclid Avenues. By Juliette Fairley | Published: 10/26/2026, 12:19:29 PM EDT Raccoon. (Unsplash) A surge in animal rabies cases across the U.S. has led federal health officials and professional veterinary organizations to issue public health warnings. From July through August, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) documented 17 percent more rabies-related inquiries than during the same period in 2025, including reports of events involving more than one person being exposed. “Several high-profile rabies outbreaks and mass rabies exposure events have highlighted the importance of performing careful rabies risk assessment,” the CDC said in a statement online. A veterinarian worker network called Vet Candy is calling for domestic pet vaccinations against rabies because infected wildlife, such as bats and raccoons, are a risk to both humans and their furry companions. For example, a cat found near 11th Street NW and Moorman Avenue NW in Roanoke, Virginia, on Oct. 9 tested positive for rabies, according to a Virginia Department of Health statement online. In California, the Pasadena Public Health Department reported finding an infected bat on Oct. 11 along East Green Street between South Marengo and South Euclid Avenues. It is the city's third reported rabid bat of the year. “Although human rabies infections remain rare in the United States, the virus continues to circulate among wildlife, creating opportunities for exposure when infected animals come into contact with people, pets, or other animals,” a Vet Candy alert states. Rabies is a zoonotic viral disease that is nearly 100 percent fatal once clinical symptoms emerge in either animals or humans. However, it is preventable with vaccination. About 100,000 Americans receive a rabies vaccination after possible exposure every year, according to the CDC, and the animals most frequently reported infected with rabies are bats, raccoons, skunks, and foxes. A pallid bat flying over a pond at night in a file photo. Shutterstock Last month, the CDC issued a Health Alert Network (HAN) health advisory in response to increases in human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals. “One of the biggest misconceptions about rabies is that infected animals always appear aggressive,” Vet Candy authorities said. “While aggression can be a clinical sign, rabid animals may also become unusually friendly, disoriented, weak, or unable to walk normally.” Once infected with a bite or scratch, health care providers can administer post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) to prevent rabies from spreading and causing death. The CDC advises clinicians that it’s important to administer PEP appropriately because errors in rabies risk assessment and PEP administration could result in potential adverse effects and avoidable costs. “For persons who have never been vaccinated against rabies, PEP should always include [human rabies immune globulin] HRIG and vaccine,” CDC authorities said. “Persons who were previously vaccinated against rabies should receive vaccine on days 0 and 3 and should not receive HRIG.”

supplementary_news.content_title: 3 raccoons test positive for rabies in North Smithfield, Pawtucket
supplementary_news.content: NORTH SMITHFIELD, R.I. (WPRI) — The Rhode Island Department of Health is warning residents in Pawtucket and North Smithfield that three raccoons have tested positive for rabies. The Health Department confirmed a rabid raccoon was found near Black Plain Road in North Smithfield this week. Two more rabid raccoons were also discovered in “close proximity to each other” near Wilcox and Blaisdell avenues, according to the Health Department. The two Pawtucket raccoons were found roughly a mile away from where another rabid raccoon was found on Hope Street in Providence last week. While there were no known human exposures to the raccoons in Pawtucket, the Health Department said a dog and two residents are receiving post-exposure treatment in North Smithfield. The Health Department has identified 46 rabid wild animals so far this year. This is nearly two times the annual average of 25 rabid animals reported between 2021 and 2025. Anyone who may have also had direct contact with the raccoons should call the Health Department’s Center for Acute Infectious Disease Epidemiology at 401-222-2577. Rabies is a potentially deadly viral disease that typically spreads through bites or scratches from an infected animal, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) . The rabies virus primarily affects the central nervous system and, if left untreated, almost always results in death. The animals most frequently infected with rabies locally are bats, skunks, raccoons and foxes, according to the Health Department. Humans who are exposed to rabies are given a series of shots over four to five weeks to ensure the virus doesn’t spread throughout the body. The CDC notes that, once the rabies virus advances past the incubation period to the onset of symptoms, there is no effective treatment for it. Rhode Island law requires dogs, cats and ferrets to be vaccinated against rabies. This not only prevents them from contracting rabies, but also spreading the disease to humans and other pets. Below are some rabies prevention tips from the Health Department: Make sure all dogs, cats and ferrets are up to date on rabies vaccinations. Avoid all contact with and do not feed stray or free-roaming domestic animals. Avoid all contact with and do not feed wild animals. Do not feed your animals outdoors, as this will attract other animals. This is especially dangerous when feeding large numbers of free-roaming cats. Protect your pets by always maintaining control; walk dogs on a leash or let them play in a fenced yard, and do not let pets wander unsupervised. Report all animal bites to your city/town’s animal control officer. Securely cover all garbage cans so wild animals cannot scavenge for food. The Health Department posts its rabies data here . Windsor, NSW Print Edition What's On HOME LATEST NEWS BUSINESS SPORT COMMUNITY PROPERTY LIFE Directory Notice Board +Health Call WIRES, don’t handle bats Health warning after rise in bites and scratches and Hawkesbury has local colonies. , and Editorial Collective October 31, 2026 . 9:37 AM 2 min read X Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Share via Email Photo by Nils Bouillard / Unsplash Hawkesbury residents are being urged to call wildlife rescuers rather than handle injured or distressed bats, following a sharp increase in people requiring medical assessment after bites and scratches. The warning has local relevance, with a flying-fox colony near the intersection of Hawkesbury Valley Way and Macquarie Street in Windsor. ABC News has reported concerns about increased encounters between people and struggling flying-foxes during a suspected food shortage along the NSW coast. NSW Health says 43 people were assessed following bat bites or scratches between September 28 and October 10, compared with 10 during the same fortnight last year. Those figures represent people assessed after contact with bats, not confirmed infections or necessarily hospital admissions. The concern is Australian bat lyssavirus, a virus closely related to rabies that can be carried by fruit bats, also known as flying-foxes, and insect-eating microbats. Human infection is extremely rare, but there is no effective treatment once symptoms develop. NSW Health’s Director in Health Protection, Keira Glasgow, urged people to leave rescues to trained handlers. “If you see a bat that is injured or in distress, call your local wildlife rescue service and do not touch it,” she said. Food shortages can cause flying-foxes to remain in backyard feeding trees during daylight instead of returning to their usual colonies. A bat seen during the day is not necessarily infected, and its appearance cannot reliably indicate whether it carries the virus. Residents who find a bat injured, grounded or caught in netting should keep children and pets away and call WIRES on 1300 094 737. They should not attempt to pick it up, untangle it or manage the rescue themselves. Anyone bitten or scratched should immediately wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water for at least 15 minutes, apply an antiviral antiseptic such as povidone-iodine, and seek urgent medical attention. This advice applies even to people previously vaccinated against rabies. Do not wait for symptoms. Simply living near a flying-fox colony or walking past roosting bats does not constitute a lyssavirus exposure. The warning concerns direct contact, particularly bites, scratches or saliva entering broken skin, the eyes, nose or mouth. Flying-foxes play an important role in pollination and seed dispersal. Calling trained rescuers helps protect both residents and wildlife. (KMIZ) A second bat has tested positive for rabies in Cole County, the Cole County Health Department announced in a Thursday press release. The first reported case was reported on Sept. 17 when a bat made contact with a stray cat, a previous press release says. Thursday’s release says a “domestic animal” was potentially exposed to the bat, but it was up to date on their rabies vaccine and received a booster. There are no known human exposures. Rabies is a virus that can spread to people and pets through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. Contact a vet as soon as possible if your pet has been exposed to rabies, the release says. The release says those who have been bitten or scratched by a potentially rabid animal should wash the wound immediately and contact your healthcare provider. By Justine Verastigue Published: Oct. 30, 2026 at 1:23 AM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google LAS VEGAS (FOX5) — Clark County officials say a victim was bitten by a rabid fox in south Las Vegas. Clark County says the fox was confirmed to have rabies Thursday evening. The victim was bitten in the 9300 block of Jeremy Blaine Court, near I-15 and Silverado Ranch Boulevard. Officials say they are alerting the public in the area who may have had contact with the fox or possibly been bitten by it to seek immediate medical attention. supplementary_news.content: Health & Fitness Rabid Raccoon Found In Old Bridge Backyard An Old Bridge resident discovered a lethargic raccoon in their backyard Sunday: OLD BRIDGE, NJ — A "lethargic" raccoon found Sunday in the backyard of an Old Bridge home died, and later tested positive for the rabies virus, announced Middlesex County. On Sunday, Oct. 25, an Old Bridge resident discovered a lethargic raccoon in their backyard, in the vicinity of West Greystone Road and Old Bridge-Englishtown Road. Animal control responded and retrieved the raccoon. The raccoon was taken to the New Jersey Department of Health Laboratory for testing. It was reported on Wednesday, October 28 that it tested positive for rabies. Find out what's happening in Matawan-Aberdeenfor free with the latest updates from Patch. There were no human exposures and no animal exposures to the raccoon. This is the fifth rabid animal reported in Middlesex County for 2026 and the first rabid animal in Old Bridge. Find out what's happening in Matawan-Aberdeenfor free with the latest updates from Patch. Residents should report wild animals showing signs of unusual behavior to their local police department. Avoid contact with wild animals and immediately report any bites from wild or domestic animals to your local health department and consult a physician as soon as possible. Keep dogs on leashes at all times and make sure they are up to date on their rabies vaccinations. Get more local news delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for free Patch newsletters and alerts
